The Ostrogoths were the eastern branch of the Gothic peoples, ruled by Theodoric the Great, who conquered and governed Italy from 493 to 526 and built a kingdom that preserved Roman institutions under Germanic leadership. Theodoric was raised in Constantinople and became known for his sophistication and learning. His kingdom was a high point of post-Roman order—he ruled Italy for more than three decades, claiming legitimacy from the Eastern Roman emperor while governing independently. He commissioned the Mausoleum of Theodoric, an imposing circular monument in Ravenna that stood as a symbol of the kingdom's grandeur and its blend of Germanic and Roman cultures. Yet beneath the surface, serious tensions simmered. The kingdom faced increasing conflict between the Catholic Roman population and Arian Gothic rulers, a religious divide that destabilized the realm. Theodoric suppressed religious dissent harshly, and his execution of the Roman senator Boethius became infamous as a symbol of cultural conflict between Roman and barbarian values. The Ostrogoths had conquered from the Huns, who had held them as tributaries, and they in turn defeated the Visigoths in regional conflicts. But their rule in Italy proved fragile. They fell to Justinian I's reconquest, a brutal Gothic War lasting from 535 to 554 that left Italy depopulated and weakened. The Ostrogoths effectively ceased to exist afterward, absorbed into Byzantine dominion.
